Chapter 7: The Age of Science, Industry, and the Loss of Certainty
Suddenly, the world was racing ahead. Steam engines thundered through the countryside, factories popped up where quiet fields used to be, and cities overflowed with people all chasing after fresh hopes. The Industrial Revolution didn’t just change how people made things—it changed how they lived, what they dreamed about, and even how they saw themselves.
Picture this: a young boy, who might’ve once followed his dad into the fields, now spends his days in a noisy mill, life measured out by the steady rhythm of turning gears. Everywhere he looks, there’s the promise of progress—people living longer, streets lit brighter, and doors opening to possibilities no one could’ve imagined before. Science and technology seemed almost magical, delivering answers and solutions at every turn.
But underneath all that excitement, something important was slipping away. The gentle pace of nature got replaced by the non-stop grind of machines. Families were uprooted, whole communities changed forever. The old comforts—faith, tradition, that deep sense of belonging—were set aside for efficiency and profit. There’s a mother working long, exhausting hours in a factory, wondering if all these sacrifices will ever give her family the safety she longs for.
Science, which once helped people understand the wonders of God’s creation, started to take center stage as the new authority. The universe began to look less like a story with purpose, and more like a giant, beautiful machine—fascinating, but kind of cold and indifferent. The old biblical way of seeing the world, full of meaning and intention, started to feel out of place in a world where everything seemed to depend on chance and cold necessity.
Imagine a scientist, peering through a microscope, totally captivated by the intricate patterns of life. Yet, when he searches for deeper meaning, all he finds are patterns and processes—no grand design, just complexity. That old search for certainty, for something solid to stand on in this whirlwind of change, suddenly felt so much harder.
As the 1800s gave way to the 1900s, the cracks in this new way of living started to show. Sure, progress brought comfort—better homes, new inventions—but it also stirred up worry and restlessness. The strange thing was, the more people discovered about the world, the less they seemed to understand about themselves. The story of Western culture became a mix: huge achievements, but also a growing sense of being lost. It’s a story full of hope, but with more than a hint of loss.
